prompt: Study the desk scene below for 15 seconds. When it disappears, answer what you remember.
stimulusText: A wooden desk sits by a window. On its surface: a closed laptop with a silver cover, a white ceramic mug half-full of coffee sitting on a cork coaster, and a stack of three paperback books, the top one with a bright red cover. A green desk lamp is switched off. To the left of the laptop lies a black ballpoint pen. A single potted succulent sits in the far corner of the desk, near a small brass alarm clock reading 9:15.
stimulusFacts: the laptop has a silver cover and is closed
the mug is white ceramic and sits on a cork coaster
there are three paperback books stacked
the top book has a red cover
the desk lamp is green and switched off
a black pen lies to the left of the laptop
a potted succulent sits in the far corner of the desk
the brass alarm clock reads 9:15

questions.prompt: How many paperback books were stacked on the desk?
questions.explanation: The scene described a stack of three paperbacks with a red-covered book on top.

questions.prompt: What color was the top book's cover?
questions.explanation: Bright colors on top of a stack are easy anchor points — naming them as you scan makes them stick.

questions.prompt: What time did the alarm clock read?
questions.explanation: Small numeric details like clock faces are often skipped in a first glance because they take an extra beat to read.

questions.prompt: True or False: the desk lamp was switched on.
questions.explanation: The lamp was described as switched off — noticing the absence of light is as useful as noticing its presence.

prompt: Study the street corner scene below for 15 seconds, then answer from memory.
stimulusText: At a quiet street corner, a red stop sign stands beside a blue mailbox. A woman in a yellow raincoat waits at the curb, holding a black umbrella that is closed. Behind her, a bicycle with a wicker basket leans against a lamppost. Two pigeons peck at the ground near a storm drain. A green sedan is parked directly beneath a 'No Parking' sign.
stimulusFacts: the stop sign is red and the mailbox is blue
the woman's raincoat is yellow
her umbrella is black and closed
a bicycle with a wicker basket leans against a lamppost
two pigeons peck near a storm drain
a green sedan is parked beneath a 'No Parking' sign

questions.prompt: What color was the woman's raincoat?
questions.explanation: Clothing color is one of the fastest details to register — and one of the fastest to forget without a deliberate label.

questions.prompt: How many pigeons were near the storm drain?
questions.explanation: Small counts of background animals or objects are a common blind spot when attention is on the person in the foreground.

questions.prompt: What was parked beneath the 'No Parking' sign?
questions.explanation: Pairing an object with the sign or landmark nearest it gives you a location anchor that's easy to recall later.

questions.prompt: True or False: the woman's umbrella was open.
questions.explanation: The umbrella was closed — a state easy to assume incorrectly if you register 'umbrella' without registering its condition.

prompt: Study this description of a man's appearance for 12 seconds, then answer from memory.
stimulusText: A man stands near the office entrance wearing a charcoal-gray suit jacket over a light-blue dress shirt, no tie. His shoes are brown leather oxfords, slightly scuffed at the left toe. A silver watch sits on his left wrist, and he carries a black leather messenger bag over his right shoulder. A small enamel pin shaped like a compass is fastened to his lapel. His hair is closely cropped and graying at the temples.
stimulusFacts: suit jacket is charcoal-gray, shirt is light-blue, no tie
shoes are brown leather oxfords, scuffed at the left toe
a silver watch is on his left wrist
a black leather messenger bag hangs over his right shoulder
a compass-shaped enamel pin is on his lapel
his hair is closely cropped and graying at the temples

questions.prompt: What shape was the lapel pin?
questions.explanation: Small accessories are exactly the kind of detail a rushed glance skips — they reward a deliberate second pass.

questions.prompt: Which shoulder was the messenger bag worn on?
questions.explanation: Noting which side of the body carries an item is a habit worth building before you ever try to interpret it.

questions.prompt: Which wrist was the watch on?
questions.explanation: Left-right details are easy to reverse in memory unless you tag them explicitly as you look.

questions.prompt: True or False: he was wearing a tie.
questions.explanation: The shirt was open-collared with no tie — absence of an expected item is a detail worth noticing, not just presence.

questions.prompt: Which shoe had the scuff mark?
questions.explanation: This is what to notice, not what it means: a scuff is a fact about wear, not evidence of character.

prompt: Study the living room scene for 12 seconds, then answer from memory.
stimulusText: A living room holds a gray sectional sofa with four throw pillows — two navy, one mustard yellow, one striped. A glass coffee table sits atop a round jute rug, holding a stack of magazines and a lit candle in a black jar. Above the fireplace hangs a framed painting of mountains. A tall bookshelf against the far wall holds exactly twelve books and a small brass telescope on its middle shelf. A gray cat sleeps on the windowsill.
stimulusFacts: the sofa is gray with four throw pillows: two navy, one mustard yellow, one striped
the glass coffee table sits on a round jute rug
the coffee table holds magazines and a lit candle in a black jar
the painting above the fireplace shows mountains
the bookshelf holds twelve books and a brass telescope on the middle shelf
a gray cat sleeps on the windowsill

questions.prompt: How many throw pillows were on the sofa?
questions.explanation: Counting items in a cluster is easier if you group them by feature (color, pattern) rather than counting one by one.

questions.prompt: How many books were on the bookshelf?
questions.explanation: Exact counts of many similar objects are hard to hold in peripheral awareness — this is a genuinely difficult recall, not a careless miss.

questions.prompt: What sat on the middle shelf besides books?
questions.explanation: An object that doesn't belong with its surroundings (a telescope among books) is naturally easier to recall than one that blends in.

questions.prompt: What was the subject of the painting above the fireplace?
questions.explanation: Wall art tends to sit in peripheral vision during a scan — this question rewards widening your gaze, not just fixating on furniture.

questions.prompt: True or False: the candle jar was black.
questions.explanation: Small color details on small objects are a common place peripheral awareness training pays off.

prompt: Memorize the order of the eight items below. You'll be asked to recall specific positions.
stimulusText: You are shown a delivery checklist, read top to bottom: 1) umbrella, 2) flashlight, 3) rope, 4) canteen, 5) map, 6) whistle, 7) matches, 8) compass.
stimulusFacts: position 1: umbrella
position 2: flashlight
position 3: rope
position 4: canteen
position 5: map
position 6: whistle
position 7: matches
position 8: compass

questions.prompt: Which item was fourth on the list?
questions.explanation: Anchoring a list to a known sequence, like counting on your fingers, helps you hold position numbers rather than just item names.

questions.prompt: What was the first item listed?
questions.explanation: The first item in a list is usually the easiest to recall — a useful checkpoint for whether your memory of the whole sequence is intact.

questions.prompt: Which item came immediately after 'rope'?
questions.explanation: Recalling adjacency (what came right after something) is a different skill from recalling absolute position, and both are worth practicing.

questions.prompt: What was the last item on the list?
questions.explanation: Like the first item, the last item benefits from a recency effect — it's worth noticing when your recall relies on that rather than genuine encoding.

prompt: Study the café scene for 10 seconds. There are more objects here than in earlier drills — expect to miss a few, and notice which ones.
stimulusText: Inside a busy cafe, a barista in a green apron steams milk behind the counter. At the nearest table, a woman types on a silver laptop next to a half-eaten croissant on a white plate. A man across from her reads a folded newspaper, a pair of round tortoiseshell glasses pushed up on his forehead. On the counter sits a chalkboard menu listing 'Espresso - $3, Latte - $4, Cold Brew - $5.' A yellow bicycle courier bag hangs from a hook by the door. Three stacked paper cups sit near the register, and a tip jar holds a handful of coins and one folded five-dollar bill.
stimulusFacts: the barista wears a green apron
the laptop on the nearest table is silver, next to a half-eaten croissant on a white plate
the man's round tortoiseshell glasses are pushed up on his forehead
the chalkboard lists Espresso $3, Latte $4, Cold Brew $5
a yellow courier bag hangs on a hook by the door
three paper cups are stacked near the register
the tip jar holds coins and one folded five-dollar bill

questions.prompt: What was the price of a Latte on the chalkboard?
questions.explanation: Text embedded in a busy scene (menu prices) is often skipped entirely when attention is drawn to people in the foreground.

questions.prompt: What color was the courier bag hanging by the door?
questions.explanation: Objects at the edge of a scene, like the bag by the door, test whether your scan reached beyond the central table.

questions.prompt: Where were the man's glasses?
questions.explanation: This is exactly the kind of small posture-adjacent detail worth training yourself to register before ever trying to interpret it.

questions.prompt: How many paper cups were stacked near the register?
questions.explanation: Small counts near a busy focal point (the register) get crowded out by more prominent details unless you deliberately scan past them.

questions.prompt: True or False: the tip jar contained a folded five-dollar bill.
questions.explanation: A single distinctive item among many similar ones (one bill among coins) is a natural anchor point once you notice it.

prompt: Each question below shows four sequences. Three follow the same rule — find the one that breaks it.

questions.prompt: Which of these four number sequences breaks the pattern followed by the others?
questions.explanation: The other three sequences all increase by a constant 3; this one increases by 3, 3, then jumps by 4, breaking the rule.

questions.prompt: Which letter sequence breaks the pattern followed by the others?
questions.explanation: ACE, BDF, and GIK each skip exactly one letter between steps; MPR skips two letters then one, breaking the consistent skip.

questions.prompt: Which of these four sequences breaks the pattern followed by the others?
questions.explanation: The first three sequences double at each step; this one adds a constant 7 instead, following an entirely different rule.

prompt: Study the street scene for 8 seconds. Details here are subtler and time is shorter — focus on scanning rather than fixating.
stimulusText: The street is crowded at midday. A cyclist in a bright orange jacket weaves between a delivery van marked 'Halden & Co.' and a parked motorcycle with a cracked side mirror. A street vendor sells pretzels from a silver cart, its umbrella striped red and white. Above the vendor, a store awning reads 'Merrow Books, Est. 1972' in faded gold letters. A traffic light hangs mid-change from yellow to red. On the far corner, a woman walks three dogs - a beagle, a poodle, and a dachshund - on a single tangled leash. A discarded newspaper page rests against a fire hydrant painted yellow with a chipped cap.
stimulusFacts: the delivery van is marked 'Halden & Co.'
the parked motorcycle has a cracked side mirror
the vendor cart is silver with a red and white striped umbrella
the awning reads 'Merrow Books, Est. 1972' in gold letters
the traffic light is mid-change from yellow to red
a woman walks a beagle, a poodle, and a dachshund on one leash
the fire hydrant is yellow with a chipped cap

questions.prompt: What name was printed on the delivery van?
questions.explanation: Business names in a busy scene are easy to lose when attention is split between multiple moving elements.

questions.prompt: What year was Merrow Books established, according to the awning?
questions.explanation: Small printed text above eye level is one of the first things a fast, low-time scan tends to drop.

questions.prompt: Which three dogs was the woman walking?
questions.explanation: Grouped items like a set of three dogs are best remembered as a labeled group rather than three separate facts.

questions.prompt: What was cracked on the parked motorcycle?
questions.explanation: A single damaged detail on an otherwise ordinary object is exactly the kind of thing a three-pass scan is built to catch.

questions.prompt: What color was the fire hydrant?
questions.explanation: Fire hydrants are usually assumed to be red by default — this one breaks that assumption, which is exactly why it's worth double-checking assumptions during a scan.

prompt: A dealer lays out ten cards in a row. Study the order for 15 seconds, then recall specific positions.
stimulusText: A dealer lays out ten cards face-up in a single row, left to right: 7 of clubs, Queen of hearts, 2 of diamonds, King of spades, 9 of clubs, Ace of hearts, 4 of spades, 10 of diamonds, Jack of clubs, 6 of hearts.
stimulusFacts: position 1: 7 of clubs
position 2: Queen of hearts
position 3: 2 of diamonds
position 4: King of spades
position 5: 9 of clubs
position 6: Ace of hearts
position 7: 4 of spades
position 8: 10 of diamonds
position 9: Jack of clubs
position 10: 6 of hearts

questions.prompt: Which card was in the fifth position?
questions.explanation: With ten items, chunking the row into groups of two or three cards makes individual positions far easier to recover.

questions.prompt: What card immediately followed the King of spades?
questions.explanation: Adjacency recall (what came right after a landmark card) is often easier than recalling an absolute position number.

questions.prompt: Which position was the Ace of hearts in?
questions.explanation: The Ace is a naturally distinctive card, which makes it a good landmark for anchoring the positions around it.

questions.prompt: What was the last card in the row?
questions.explanation: The final item in a sequence usually benefits from a recency effect — worth noting if that's the only reason you recalled it correctly.

prompt: Study the cluttered desk for only 6 seconds. This is the hardest sprint in the set — expect to miss details, and treat every correct answer as a real win.
stimulusText: A cluttered office desk holds a chaos of items: a laptop open to a spreadsheet, a mug with a chipped handle reading 'World's Okayest Boss,' a tangle of three charging cables (one red, one white, one braided gray), a stack of seven manila folders with one labeled 'URGENT' in red marker, a pair of scissors stuck point-down into a pen cup, a sticky note reading '3pm - call Dana' stuck to the monitor's bottom-left corner, a half-empty water bottle with a cracked cap, and a small potted cactus missing one spine on its left side. A calendar on the wall behind shows the month of March with the 14th circled in blue ink.
stimulusFacts: the mug reads 'World's Okayest Boss' and has a chipped handle
three charging cables are tangled together: one red, one white, one braided gray
there is a stack of seven manila folders, one labeled 'URGENT' in red marker
scissors are stuck point-down into a pen cup
a sticky note reads '3pm - call Dana' on the monitor's bottom-left corner
the water bottle is half-empty with a cracked cap
the potted cactus is missing one spine on its left side
the wall calendar shows March with the 14th circled in blue ink

questions.prompt: What did the mug say?
questions.explanation: Text on an object competes with a dozen other details for the same fraction of a second — catching it at all is the point of this drill.

questions.prompt: How many manila folders were stacked on the desk?
questions.explanation: Exact counts under six seconds are genuinely difficult; the goal is to notice you're estimating rather than assume you counted precisely.

questions.prompt: What did the sticky note say?
questions.explanation: A sticky note tucked in a corner of the monitor is a classic missed detail — it rewards scanning the full frame, not just the desk surface.

questions.prompt: Which date was circled on the calendar?
questions.explanation: Background details on a wall, away from the main clutter, are exactly what a widened, non-fixated gaze is trained to catch.

questions.prompt: True or False: the cactus was missing a spine on its right side.
questions.explanation: The missing spine was on the left side — a reminder that left/right details are the easiest to flip in memory under time pressure.
